In December 2017, a news story broke warning that “the Arctic will never be frozen again.” Recycling the trope “What happens in the Arctic does not stay in the Arctic,” journalists picked up comments by lead- ing scientists attached to a US agency, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). In their annual Arctic Report Card, NOAA declared that “the Arctic shows no sign of returning to [the] reliably frozen region of recent decades” (Holthaus 2017).

The idea of the Arctic being a “reliably frozen region” caught our collective eyes for four reasons. First, how and why does reliability matter and what happens when something or someplace becomes unreliable? The news story implied that geographical knowledge and scientific understanding becomes scrambled (Dodds and Nuttall 2016). Second, the reference to “frozen” seems an apt descriptor for a region that until quite recently was widely considered and represented as a “frozen desert,” remote and/or sparsely populated with limited communicative infrastruc- ture (Koivurova 2010). Third, it was widely seen to have a material abundance of ice and snow alongside environmental characteristics such as cold and harshness. If ice and cold are no longer “reliable” then what implications does that hold for the spatial politics of the Arctic? Finally, how might such a descriptor usefully inform this edited book’s mission, which is a cross-disciplinary encounter with the region itself, with due attention to what one scholar terms a “Multiplex World” (Acharya 2014)?

In our reading of the Arctic as region, we make a broader point about the need to take seriously the role of the material as more than simply constituting a passive physical landscape and seascape. For political geographers, the spatial politics of the region is not something to be taken for granted. As John Agnew warned his audience, there are “territorial traps” that lie in wait for the unwary (Agnew 1994, 2013). Territory, terrain, region, border and scale are not self-evident or immutable. In Agnew’s conception, space is a space for action, a source of controversy and complicit always with knowledge-power relationships and regimes. While IR scholars distinguish between distinct levels of analysis (e.g. local, national, regional and global) and work with defined regional spaces (e.g. Africa, Europe, Mediterranean), geographical research on regions and the regional address mul- tiple, interlocking scalar and spatial frames of reference (Söderbaum 2016). As Stuart Elden reminds us, terms such as territory and terrain demand careful genea- logical investigation – the meaning, scope and extent vary over time and space (Elden 2017).

More recent work has been inspired by two strands that have relevance for those interested in the spatial politics of the region – materiality and volume ontologies (Squire 2015). Moving beyond debates about whether a region is ter- ritorial (rooted) or networked (routed), the focus is more on how elements such as ice and water are generative of geopolitical agency and the potent imaginative geographies of the Arctic as a space for regional politics. In our reading, material elements and forces are integral to spatial politics and capable of disrupting geo- political notions of “reliably frozen regions.” Building on a material turn in politi- cal geography, recent scholarship has called for a view of territory as volumetric, where height, depth, terrain, altitude and pressure complicate our understandings of the spatial and territorial (Steinberg and Peters 2015).

. More fundamentally, simply acknowledging that “the Arctic” exists at all is likely to reveal the role of social and political practices that enable its invention, deployment and even dissolution. It is also likely to reveal an under-accounted for material politics. If the “region” is viewed as a social/discursive construction and a political performance, a variety of spatial scales from the local and sub-national to the international and global are mobilised, largely oblivious to material quali- ties of the inanimate materials and the non-human world (Dittmer 2017). Spatial imaginaries proceed to frame understandings, orientations and direct particular spatial projects such as the establishment of regional bodies, the work of states and other stakeholders within particular regions and the management of extra- regional parties.

When the Arctic as “region” is scrutinised by scholars from geography, politi- cal science, law, IR and anthropology there are two dominant strands (Keskitalo 2007). The first takes an institutional focus and explores how intergovernmental forums, such as the Arctic Council and Barents Euro-Arctic Council, were piv- otal in creating distinctly actors and issues. Within this literary corpus, academics disagree whether Arctic governance is akin to a regime, bazaar and/or mosaic with associated implications for how insiders and outsiders are defined, regulated and policed (Keil and Knecht 2017). The second considers how different geo- graphical imaginaries have played their part in generating multiple Arctic(s) – as homeland, as wilderness, as resource frontier, as scientific hub and as zone of peace and cooperation (Steinberg, Tasch, and Gerhardt 2015). Complicating mat- ters further, there are also distinct national/regional traditions which inter-change the Arctic with the “High North” and simply “North.” For Norwegians, the High North is a region encompassing Greenland, the Nordic Arctic and western Russia. For Canadians, the North refers to land and sea north of 60 degrees North rather than 66 degrees North (Arctic Circle). The Arctic as region gets imagined and put to work in multiple ways but it rarely embraces the manner in which the material generates imaginations and the inter-connectivity of the elemental in the form of ice, snow, water and rock.

2. Central Arctic ocean as emerging region?

The opening section considered how the Arctic as a material volume offers insights into how the intersection between human actors and the marine environment is generating subterranean and submarine interventions. International law (in the form of the United Nations Law of the Sea Convention, UNCLOS in particular) has been pivotal in staging a series of encounters between coastal and non-coastal states, geophysical sciences and the Arctic seabed and submarine environments. Diminishing sea ice, ice sheet melting and the prospect of sea level change have contributed to an unprecedented level of debate and reflection on a “warming Arc- tic” and a “melting Arctic.” Arctic states, aided and abetted by specific articles in UNCLOS on ice-covered waters (Article 234) and extended continental shelves (Article 76), are committed to extending their sovereign rights over the seabed of the Arctic Ocean, and dedicated to maintaining an active managerial grip on the shipping routes off the northern territories of Canada (Northwest Passage) and Russia (Northern Sea Route). The material condition of the Arctic, in the form of ice-covered waters, was generative not only of international legal provisions but also of spatial interventions by coastal states in the form of movement, surveil- lance and defence. What UNCLOS did not consider, however, was whether those ice-covered waters might no longer be covered with ice in decades to come. Open water treats human agency differently to ice-covered waters. Simply put, ice tends to block and complicate activities such as resource extraction and shipping.

The latest AMAP report entitled “Snow, Water, Ice and Permafrost in the Arc- tic” (2017) stipulates the scale and scope of change affecting the Arctic region, specifically the ice-water ratio in the Arctic Ocean (AMAP 2017). The prospect of a summer ice-free Arctic Ocean had yet to be imagined or encountered. Within the last 15 years, however, areas once considered beyond the realm of the human appear amenable to the colonisation and exploitation of states. The outer continen- tal shelves of the Arctic Ocean are international waters, which either fall within the preserve of coastal states or are areas that extend beyond national jurisdiction (ABNJ). In 2017, member states of the UN recommended that there should be an internationally binding agreement on marine biodiversity in the central Arctic Ocean (CAO). This follows an earlier resolution in 2015 to develop an interna- tional legally binding instrument compatible with UNCLOS. Such a treaty would have implications for the material politics of CAO gov- ernance, where the subterranean and the submarine are subject to new forms of geopolitical and legal intervention (Pan and Huntington 2016). The resolu- tion coincides with the existing negotiations between the Arctic Ocean coastal states (A5) and five extra-territorial parties, including China and the EU, over the possibility of commercial fishing in the CAO. The impulse for such negotia- tions is material state-change underwritten by the loss of sea ice, the warming of open water and the migratory drift northwards of fish stocks. The A5 have urged a precautionary approach and signed the 2015 Oslo Declaration Concern- ing the Prevention of Unregulated High Seas Fishing in the Central Arctic Ocean. The declaration argues that fishing should be prevented until scientific research and management could ensure sustainable fisheries.

The opening up of the CAO as a prospective fishing ground, or as a sanctuary for fragile fisheries is thus more than just a political, legal or economic matter. As with representations of the Frozen North or the Polar Mediterranean, the CAO is connected to material shifts such as ice loss and shrinkage combined with the generation of new cartographies of the Arctic Ocean that highlight the presence of open water and thinning sea ice rather than a solid, frozen desert. What the nego- tiations are likely to work towards is the development of a regional fisheries man- agement organisation (RFMO). If a RFMO for the CAO does come to fruition, then it is going to build upon and co-exist with a host of pre-existing oceanic zon- ings: high seas, exclusive economic zones, outer continental shelves, territorial waters. While a RFMO in the CAO may solve some problems, its efficacy will remain constrained by the ocean’s incessant dynamism: ice floes, fish and water molecules all move. Thus, even as the CAO is “opened up” for fishing and for new institutions of regulatory intervention, these interventions may well “close” it through the drawing of lines between ice and water, between ice and land, and between the CAO and adjacent, but intimately interconnected, seas. Thus, the potential legacy of this effort to fill policy and knowledge gaps may end up being a division of the elements and ecologies that it is supposed to interconnect. While the Arctic Ocean has only been comparatively recently recognised as a discreet ocean, it might be better conceived as an interlocking element in a series of spaces that make up the Arctic and beyond (for example, Sorlin 2018). As the migrations of the region’s indigenous inhabitants and its non-human actors such as whales and seabirds, as well as the circulation of water itself remind us, the Arctic Ocean is but one element in a wider network of migration and interac- tion. So, conventional maps of the CAO need not tether our imaginations when it comes to thinking of those boundaries as fundamentally porous. Where the CAO begins and ends could be a far more unrestricted and more provocative question, and recent research suggests that increased shipping in the Arctic Ocean brings with it further potential to cause physical change. In short, the ongoing negotiations regarding the CAO might act as a more gen- eral prompt for thinking of the Arctic as a region, which is both porous and flow- ing as well as bordered and rooted. Thinking of the Arctic as a regional volume alerts us to how flows of air, water, ice and non-human agents shape and pull our understandings of the Arctic both as a territorial space but also as something more relational. Sea level change, diminishing sea ice, ocean acidification and migratory flows of fish and other animals already give us clues as to how the Arc- tic Ocean is intimately linked to the world’s other oceans, landforms and global atmosphere. This would seem to be emblematic of calls for critical ocean studies and, what we would term, critical ice studies (DeLoughrey 2017; Dodds 2018).

Terms such as the “Canadian Arctic,” the “American Arctic” and the “Russian Arctic” remain powerful constructions highlighting the colonisation and nationalisation of land, ice and snow and its human and non- human inhabitants. Those acts of settler colonialism were also underwritten by material encounters and experiences. The Arctic as a contact zone, imaginative and embodied, remains ongoing and contested as indigenous peoples continue to campaign over land claims, and demand greater autonomy, consultation and social justice (Wormbs 2018).

In an earlier publication, one of the authors working with Arctic anthropolo- gist Mark Nuttall, argued that in the last decade and a half the Arctic has become “scrambled” in a sense that the Arctic, and even more specifically the Arctic Ocean, is no longer reliably characterised as inaccessible, frozen or even lifeless and certainly not beyond the realm of human intervention (Dodds and Nuttall 2019). While there have been limited human crossings by and trading networks of indigenous inhabitants and explorers/scientists, historically the regional geographies of the Arctic were lively and dynamic as whalers, seal- ers, travellers and traders made their mark on northern communities and more than human life.

In 1921, the International Hydrographic Organization (IHO) formally recog- nised the Arctic as an ocean (see Figure 8.2). About the same time nation-states both below and above the Arctic Circle negotiated the Svalbard Treaty (entered into force 1925 and established a legal regime for the management of the archi- pelago Svalbard as a Norwegian national territory with guaranteed rights for third party signatories such as Russia and the United Kingdom) and in some cases projected national ambitions towards the North Pole (Canada and Rus- sia via sector theory, using lines of latitude to extend national territories ever northwards). The IHO identification of the Arctic as ocean-space rather than a point on the map where latitudinal lines converge is significant. But what this two-dimensional definition did not address, however, was oceanic volume – the height and depth of ocean lay beyond the legal and geopolitical grip of states. The Arctic, as Figure 8.2 suggests, is defined as a zone rather than a volume (Steinberg 2010).

Through their extensive patrolling and infrastructural investment, in combination with support for Arctic science, both the United States and the Soviet Union reimagined the Arc- tic as a more integrated, volumetric and coherent regional space, that the British geographers Terence Armstrong and his colleagues described as a “circumpolar North” in 1978 (Armstrong, Rogers, and Rowley 1978).

For Armstrong, however, the rationale for “circumpolar North” was not just rooted in Cold War geopolitical machinations but also growing evidence of transnational indigenous activism and environmental cooperation in areas such as polar bear conservation. From Alaska to Scandinavia, indigenous communi- ties were articulating demands for greater autonomy and cultural recognition. In 1977 the Inuit Circumpolar Conference brought Alaskan, Soviet, Greenlandic and Canadian representatives together to consider shared interests and values across the northern coastal territories and seas (Nicol 2010). But a “circumpolar North” is rather different to thinking of the Arctic as a volume.

While Gorbachev’s oft-cited speech draws attention to continental convergence, it is resolutely not a volumetric understanding of the Arctic. The Arctic Ocean is significant regionally speaking because the extreme edges of land converge on it. The Arctic Environment Protection Strategy (AEPS) initiated by Finland in 1991 and the Arctic Council championed by Canada played a key role in operation- alising these new regional articulations – the Arctic as a shared regional space. One important outcome was to define eight “Arctic states” namely, Canada, Denmark/Greenland, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Russia, Sweden and the United States (Arctic 8 or A8), and thus by association to identify non-Arctic states and extra-territorial actors. As the preamble to the AEPS notes, the signatories drew attention to the presence of pollutants on rather than in and through “fragile Arctic ecosystems”:

Claims to geographical proximity and environmental stewardship trumped other ways of conceiving of the Arctic as networked, relational and volumetric. Historic Arctic states such as the UK, the Netherlands, Germany and France were reclas- sified as “observers” when they entered into a relationship with the new Arctic states and the AEPS and Arctic Council respectively. The designator non-Arctic was an important element in the institutional building process even if it was per- fectly clear that the volumetric boundaries of the Arctic were rather more porous. Indeed, one of the driving factors behind the AEPS was a recognition that the Arctic was a net receiver of extra-territorial pollutants from southern countries such as the UK in the form of acid rain and persistent organic pollutants.

Perhaps it is no coincidence that as international interest in the Arctic has grown over the last two decades, so descriptors of the region have altered. Notably, the term “global Arctic” has been used to capture the manner in which economic, political and cultural forms of globalisation have interacted, even intruded, into the economies and societies of northern communities. We posit the claim that “global Arctic” has found favour with some commentators precisely because it uses the “global” to signify a more implicit sense of the volumetric akin to a leaky container (Finger and Heininen 2019). While we should be careful not to overstate these interactions, in terms of scale, scope and novelty, it evokes a changing mate- rial relationship between the Arctic and the rest of the world.

To some, the annual Arctic Circle event hosted in Iceland might be understood as welcoming an array of stakeholders and interested parties from inside and outside of the Arctic region, eager to promote, discuss and implement political, commercial and cultural agendas. . Indigenous communities have also used the global in the form of the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples to “globalise” the Arctic. In this case, the entanglement of the Arctic and the global is a deliberate one, designed to highlight indigenous peoples’ rights and the responsibilities of nation-states to treat them with respect, dignity and be attentive to outstanding land claims and natural resource arrangements. It is also important to recognise that indigenous peoples are also global actors in their own right, with cultural, economic and political portfolios, which include collective rights (Nicol 2017).

Hence, as such, there is no one “Global Arctic” per se; rather there are multi- ple, overlapping “Global Arctic(s)” that can be shored up (individually or collec- tively) at specific moments in time to serve particular interests. What is also worth considering here are the ways in which a “Global Arctic” no longer represents a remote, faraway space that is bestowed an “exceptional” and “special” status for its value towards “global” scientific investigations and explorations; rather it is increasingly rendered banal and visible as an interconnected region through com- peting narratives and agendas from within and beyond.

This is particularly related to the understanding of the Arctic as being a shared yet vul- nerable space that should be subjected to careful interventions by geographically proximate actors (as mentioned in the previous section). What this essentially means is that certain state and non-state actors are privileged in such imaginings to be involved in Arctic governance regimes (like the Ottawa Declaration). The identification of “sustainable development” and “environmental protection” as foci for the Council was rooted in the legacies and consequences of Cold War militarism and post-Cold War regional collaboration and confidence building, as exemplified by the speech in Murmansk by Premier Gorbachev in 1987 call- ing for the Arctic to be a “zone of peace” followed by the Arctic Environment Protection Strategy (AEPS) negotiated in 1991. The AEPS addressed common environmental challenges, acknowledged the agency of indigenous peoples and identified transnational pollution (such as lingering nuclear radioactivity and air- borne contaminants) as regional priorities. It did not specify an Arctic region per se. The Ottawa Declaration did not define the Arctic as a region but rather identi- fied eight Arctic states and six indigenous peoples’ organisations as members and Permanent Participants of the Arctic Council.

As scholars such as Keskitalo (2004) recognised, the Ottawa Declaration emerged at a time of Arctic “regional-speak,” with multiple Arctic(s) in conversa- tion with one another depending on geographical, ecological, legal and political criteria (Young 2005). For example, the International Arctic Science Commit- tee was created in 1990 and the Northern Research Forum established in 1999. The University of the Arctic was launched in 2001. In Oran Young’s terms, this was indicative of a move towards “mosaic co-operation.” The working groups attached to the Arctic Council, such as the Arctic Monitoring and Assessment Programme and the Conservation of Arctic Flora and Fauna, adopt different Arc- tic boundaries, with countries like Iceland occupying a liminal space between Arctic and near-Arctic and variation in how far the Arctic region extends over the northern fringes of the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. So, in terms of advancing the core agenda of the Arctic Council, the working groups and taskforces addressing matters such as marine and scientific cooperation have co-opted different working definitions of the Arctic as region. Promoting a circumpolar framing (by evoking the statist presence of eight Arctic countries interwoven by transnational indig- enous peoples) and informed by this scientific-technical knowledge producing architecture, the Arctic Council has been integral to producing the Arctic as space of shared governance (Keil and Knecht 2017).

The Declaration highlights both a shared and volumetric ocean-territory but also a legal-judicial framework in the form of the “Law of the Sea” – helping to man- age and resolve present and future challenges including the delimitation of the outer limits of the continental shelves of coastal states. While other Arctic states, such as Iceland, registered their displeasure at this initiative, fearing a geopolitics of exclusion, the Arctic 5 established a regional bloc that, while attentive to the regional, was also keenly aware of national interests and their individual sover- eign rights as coastal states (Dodds and Ingimundarson 2012).

State sovereignty and sovereign rights continue to be emphasised by all the Arc- tic states, and in particular by the A5. Article 76 of UNCLOS and the mechanism for the delimitation of outer limits of continental shelves encouraged substantial investment in oceanographic and geophysical mapping of the Arctic Ocean by the Arctic 5. The Arctic Ocean coastal states have all submitted materials to the UN Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf (CLCS), with the excep- tion of the United States, which has still not ratified UNCLOS. Environmental change coupled with the febrile reactions to the planting of a Russian flag on the seabed of the central Arctic Ocean prompted the 2008 Ilulissat Declaration as a device intended to defuse speculation that the Arctic was thinly governed and about to be scrambled over. While the UNCLOS-related process has been “orderly,” it enables and constrains particular forms of regional cooperation. Den- mark, Canada and Russia have, for example, consulted one another over their respective submissions to the CLCS and the A5 have initiated plans to work with other stakeholders about how to manage the central Arctic Ocean (international waters) should fishing become possible in the future. But the fact remained that the other Arctic states were unhappy with what they perceived to be exclusionary tactics and strategies.

Notwithstanding the common purpose of the A5 with regard to Arctic Ocean governance, the A8 were able to conjure up regional alignment by focusing on the prospect of future observers to the Arctic Council. The 1996 Ottawa Declaration made reference to:
Observer status in the Arctic Council is open to: a non-Arctic states; b intergovernmental and inter-parliamentary organisations, global and regional; and c non-governmental organisations.

The most challenging moment for the Arctic Council came at the Ministerial Meeting in 2013 when the Arctic states and Permanent Participants discussed the applications of six states and other applicants including Greenpeace and the Oil and Gas Producers Association. The six states (China, India, Singapore, Korea, Italy and Japan) were admitted at the meeting while others including the European Union (at the time an ad hoc observer) were not considered. The decision to admit five “Asian” observers marked a shift from the existing pattern of state observers, which were overwhelmingly “European” members including UK, Germany and Poland. At the same time, the eight Arctic states agreed to a legally binding oil spill response agreement, which complemented an earlier agreement on search and rescue in the Arctic region (Steinberg and Dodds 2015).

As part of the expansion of state observers, the Arctic Council revisited their guidelines (the so-called “Nuuk criteria”) for observers. Developed in 2011, they were revisited in 2013 and revised again in 2016, but in essence, it insists that observers respect the sovereignty, sovereign rights and jurisdiction of the eight states, that they contribute positively to the work of the Arctic Council and that they are not permanent observers. Notably, the observers to the Arctic Council are asked to embrace a more material and volumetric conception of the Arctic; a space with seabed, open water and surface where coastal states such as Russia and Norway enjoy sovereign rights over at least part of it. Whereas in the past, Arc- tic states might have spoken about the Arctic being defined by lines of latitudes (e.g. Arctic Circle), spherical qualities (e.g. circumpolar) and/or biogeographical markers such as the northern extent of a treeline, we have something materially and volumetrically quite different. Legal regimes such as UNCLOS are produc- tive of potent material-discursive expressions of the Arctic.

The admittance of new observers to the Arctic Council in May 2013 brought to the fore different projects – a regionalism rooted in and shaped by the Arctic states and Permanent Participants and a vision of a global Arctic where extra-territorial states such as China and Japan were now imagining themselves as “near-Arctic” states (Bennett 2015). As we argued earlier, such imaginings of a “Global Arc- tic” are often purposefully evoked to typecast the Arctic region as not necessarily bounded and can be connected to other places and peoples through various pro- cesses and performances. In particular, a medley of issues such as climate change, shipping and living and non-living resources have enabled different Arctic(s) to become the basis for intersecting regional projects.

Two things have followed from the onset of a crisis in the West’s relationship with Russia. First, the activities of the Arctic Council have endured, but specific issues, like the application of the EU for observer status, have been abandoned for the moment as a consequence of EU sanctions against Russia. In retrospect, there was a period between 2008–2014 when the Arctic states were able to con- solidate their collective regional interests, address growing extra-regional inter- est in the Arctic and cement their dominant role in Arctic governance. Legally binding agreements have been secured in the following areas: Agreement on Cooperation on Aeronautical and Maritime Search and Rescue in the Arctic (2011), Agreement on Cooperation on Marine Oil Pollution, Preparedness and Response in the Arctic (2013) and the Agreement on Enhancing Arctic Scientific Cooperation (2017). The Arctic states arguably also agreed that the admittance of additional state observers, such as China and Korea, was a useful way of consolidating their sovereign authority (Steinberg and Dodds 2015). Second, as a consequence of sanctions, Russia has looked to other partners, such as China and Vietnam, to support its oil and gas sector and encouraged changes in stakeholder involvement as western companies, such as Exxon-Mobil and BP, have pulled out of Russian partnership deals.

Until the Ukraine crisis and the consequential sanctions (such as travel restrictions) placed on Russia and its officials, we might have concluded by stating that there is evi- dence of a “regional community” forming around the Arctic region, centred on the Arctic Council. There are degrees and levels of what might be termed “region- ness,” but we could point to a community of states and Permanent Participants working in a context characterised by working groups/taskforces investigating the politics, ecologies and cultures of the Arctic region, supported by a permanent secretariat and working with an architecture characterised by ministerial meet- ings, Permanent Participants and Senior Arctic Officials attached to the eight Arctic states, and stakeholder engagement involving states, NGOs and IGOs.

, Arctic regionalism has a resilient quality and scope to it that few would have imagined possible in the mid to late 1980s, when Premier Gorbachev called for a new vision for the Arctic. Importantly, however, when the parties came together to negotiate the Ottawa Convention it seems likely that very few anticipated that the “Arctic region” would attract the kind of global interest that it does now. The last ten years have witnessed, in short, an acceleration and intensification of Arctic regionalism, which serves as a reminder that there are multiple materialities, temporalities and spatialities at play (Steinberg and Peters 2015).

This chapter has traced the making and remaking of the Arctic as a region by demonstrating the ways in which changing imaginaries and institutional develop- ments related to the Arctic are complicit in this process. Building on the claim that the Arctic can no longer be seen as “reliably frozen,” we argue that this “new” material condition pertaining to the Arctic has ushered in a more dynamic and volumetric conception of space which in turn enables different kinds of networks, practices and representations to reconstitute (meanings of) the “region.” In par- ticular, we contend that the historical associations of the Arctic as a remote, dor- mant, lifeless and unchanging region have been disrupted as a result of the marked transformations brought about by climate change and the accompanying melting of sea ice. This has essentially brought about the “awakening” of the region not only in terms of the fluctuations in its climatic and aquatic rhythms. More impor- tantly,

Indeed, the changing materialities of the Arctic have raised questions regard- ing the ownership and governance of resources and shipping routes as well as the wider impacts of climate change and sea level rise on “other” places. The rheto- ric of a “Global Arctic” has constantly been mobilised to reflect the increasingly porous, relational and networked nature of the Arctic region that necessitates the attention of the world community. It seems far removed from those more banal references to lines of latitude and biogeographical indictors of the “north.” As Steinberg and Kristoffersen (2017) demonstrate, even physical markers such as the edge of sea ice are never politically innocent. They are entangled in the state- making practices of Canada and Norway. Mapping the sea ice edge is crucial to the regulation of oil and gas exploitation, and those maps struggle to capture the dynamism they purport to represent.

Crucially, various Arctic state have been quick to appeal to international legal frameworks (e.g. UNCLOS) on top of coming up with new institutions and trea- ties (including the Arctic Council and Ottawa Declaration) to eschew an open and free-floating approach in handling Arctic (“external”) interventions, thereby ena- bling them to “fix” certain ground rules to harden their territorial and sovereign grip on the region and prioritise their interests over “others.” What we argue is that those interventions are informed by more explicitly material and volumetric interventions in the Arctic.

Hence, through this study, we align to broader debates in Political Geography, International Relations and of Arctic as a region productive of what they purport to describe, but they also invite Area Studies in not treating the region as some- thing “given” or having an ontological reality (Sidaway et al. 2016). Instead, we emphasise that there is no single, stable, hegemonic understanding of the Arc- tic region and a variety of visions exist in circulation, embodying rather diverse social interests. What this suggests is that the Arctic region has no straightforward sum and substance – it is rendered meaningful and real through a complex system of material encounters, representations and practices. Ice, snow, rock and air are integral to the production of space, the articulation of identities and embedded into the legacies of colonialism, Cold War and post-Cold War geopolitics and governance.

A critical task of prospective works on the Arctic, and we would suggest on other parts of the world that are described as regions and regional, is the speci- fication of how different material encounters and volumetric imaginaries of the region are produced, circulated and with what consequences.
